# Trend-Conditional Hedging — is "don't hedge too early" worth anything?

**Owner:** quant (path-dependent hedging). **Files:** `fxgamma/portfolio/ratchet.py`,
`fxgamma/data/intraday_yahoo.py`, this document.
**Reads against:** `08_overnight_gamma.md` (brief + both amendments), `10_forecast_evaluation.md`,
`11_overnight_desk_spec.md`, `09_hedging_theory.md`, `fxgamma/portfolio/bandopt.py`.
**Data:** all figures are from the offline synthetic paths generated by the functions named in
each section, at the seeds stated. Market-data hosts are blocked in this build; nothing here is
measured on real FX and §11 says exactly what to run when it can be.

---

## 0. Verdict, up front

The user's question is the right question and the mechanism is real:

> *"Depends if you predict the trend will continue, ie if it keeps going one direction you want to
> optimise the level dynamically so that we don't hedge too early."*

A trending path genuinely does pay a gamma book more if you hedge late, and a choppy one pays more
if you hedge often, at identical total variance. The PM's table is reproduced exactly (§2).

**But the answer to "should you trade on it" is no, and the reason is not that the effect is
absent — it is that it cannot be known in advance and it is smaller than the noise it lives in.**

| question | answer | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Is the trend effect real? | **Yes**, and it is exactly the return autocovariance | §1, §2 |
| Is intraday persistence *detectable*? | **Yes, but only pooled over ~20-250 nights** | §5 |
| Is it *forecastable* for tonight? | **No.** Beaten by the Brownian null in 7 of 7 cells, including when the true persistence is constant and large | §6 |
| Does a ratchet beat a **risk-matched** symmetric band? | Only if `phi > +0.02`, and only detectably above `phi = +0.10`; it is a **pure bet on persistence**, paying `199 x phi - 4` USD a night | §7 |
| What does being wrong cost? | The mirror image: **-25 USD/night at `phi = -0.10`, -69 at `phi = -0.30`** | §7 |
| Could the user ever verify it on their own book? | **No.** At a plausible `phi = 0.05` it takes **149 years** of nights to establish the P&L edge at t=2 | §9 |

**Recommendation: run a symmetric band, set it from the delta cap, and spend the attention on the
cap.** Ship `Ratchet` in the library, **off**, with the regime table on the screen next to it so
that anyone who turns it on can see what they are betting. The one asymmetry that *is* justified is
the one the trader already identified (§9.3 of `docs/11`): **book skew**, which is repricing and not
a view, and `AsymmetricBand` carries the sentence that says so.

This agrees with the band agent's conclusion from the other direction — the objective is so flat
that being 30% off the optimal band costs 0.1-0.9% of the gamma P&L — and with the trader's: the
band is worth tens of dollars a night, the delta cap is worth thousands.

---

## 1. The maths: what a trend-conditional rule can possibly be paid

Over a window the delta-hedged P&L is, to second order,

```
P&L = 0.5 * G * sum_over_legs (S_hedge_i - S_hedge_{i-1})^2  -  theta * tau
```

where a **leg** is the spot move between two consecutive hedges and `G = d(delta_base)/dS`. Squares
are not additive — `(a+b)^2 > a^2 + b^2` for same-sign legs, `< ` for opposite-sign — which is the
whole of the user's intuition and it is correct.

Write a leg out in its per-step returns `r_i`. Since `(sum r_i)^2 = sum r_i^2 + 2 sum_{i<j} r_i r_j`,

```
capture  =  QV  +  2 * sum_{legs} sum_{i<j in the same leg} r_i r_j          (EXACT, per path)
```

`ratchet.capture_decomposition` verifies this to machine precision (residual `0.0` on every path
tested). `QV` — the quadratic variation — is fixed by the volatility and **no hedging rule can
change it**. Therefore:

> **Every penny a trend-conditional rule can earn is the sum of the return autocovariances inside
> its own hedge legs.** In expectation `E[capture] - QV = 2 * sum gamma(j-i)`, with
> `gamma(k) = Cov(r_t, r_{t+k})`.

Three consequences that frame the rest of the document:

1. **On a martingale the expected gain of any such rule is exactly zero.** A ratchet that "lets
   winners run" on a random walk is a momentum position in disguise with zero expected P&L, extra
   cost and a fatter tail. This is the band-independence result, stated so it can be checked.
2. **The forecast target is the variance ratio** `VR(n) = Var(n-sum)/(n Var(r))`, whose reciprocal is
   exactly the roughness `kappa = QV/D^2` that `signals.rangeforecast` already computes. So this is
   the *same statistic* `docs/10` §5.4 ruled unforecastable from daily bars — which is why this work
   needed intraday data and why `fxgamma/data/intraday_yahoo.py` exists.
3. **The prize is bounded and knowable.** At an infinitely wide band the capture ratio tends to
   `VR`, so a night with `VR = 1.10` has at most 10% more gamma P&L available to a perfect
   late-hedger than to a continuous one. `ratchet.capture_ceiling` prints it in money: on the
   reference book that is **USD 169 a night**, before cost, before the delta you must carry, and
   before the possibility of being wrong.

## 2. Reproduction of the PM's table — and one convention worth knowing

`ratchet.pm_table(n_paths=4000, n_steps=240, seed=20260909)`. AR(1)-in-returns paths with the
**per-step variance equalised across phi**, so the quadratic variation is identical in every cell
and only the ordering of the moves differs. Bands are in units of one step's sd; each cell is the
mean captured sum of squared moves between hedges.

| band | trending φ=+0.3 | random walk | choppy φ=−0.3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.25 | **240.9** ± 0.4  (PM 240.6) | **239.9** ± 0.4  (240.0) | **238.4** ± 0.4  (239.4) |
| 1.00 | **261.9** ± 0.5  (261.5) | **239.9** ± 0.4  (240.1) | **214.7** ± 0.4  (215.8) |
| 2.00 | **303.9** ± 0.7  (302.8) | **239.6** ± 0.6  (239.4) | **174.3** ± 0.5  (173.9) |
| 4.00 | **349.4** ± 1.2  (348.1) | **238.0** ± 0.9  (237.0) | **146.6** ± 0.7  (148.4) |

**Reproduced**, every cell within 1-2 standard errors, and the flat random-walk column is the
textbook band-independence sanity check.

One finding fell out of the reproduction. The PM's random-walk column reads **237.0** at a 4-sigma
band rather than 240. That is not a band effect: it is the **open leg**. Counting only *completed*
legs drops the unhedged move still running at the end of the path, which is worth ~3 units at a
4-sigma band and ~0 at a 0.25-sigma band. Include it (`include_open_leg=True`) and the column is
flat at 239.9 / 240.1 / 240.5 / 241.2 — band-independence holding exactly. Both conventions are
defensible (the open leg is unrealised, but it is real money marked to market); what matters is that
**a rule that hedges less often will look ~1% worse under the completed-legs convention for a
purely mechanical reason.** Every comparison in this document therefore marks the open leg.

---

## 3. The rules, and whether they can actually be left overnight

`ratchet.py` implements four trigger rules. Each carries `.orderability`, because a rule the user
cannot type in at 17:00 and go to bed on is not a rule for this user.

| rule | what it does | what the platform must support |
|---|---|---|
| `SymmetricBand(h)` | hedge at ±`h` from the last hedge. **The baseline** — this is `bandopt.optimal_band`, or the delta cap, expressed as orders | two resting limits. **Leaveable** |
| `AsymmetricBand(h_up, h_dn, source)` | different distances each side, `source` records *why* | two resting limits. **Leaveable** |
| `Ratchet(h, give_back)` | arm at ±`h`, then trail the trigger `give_back * h` behind the running extreme | **server-side trailing stop**, or an OCO chain, or someone awake. **NOT leaveable as static limits** |
| `TimeAndState(h0, widen, tighten, max_steps)` | widen after a same-sign leg, tighten after a reversal, hedge unconditionally after `max_steps` bars | conditional / amend-on-fill order chain |

This is a first-order practical objection and it is worth stating before any P&L: **the user is
asleep.** The entire value proposition of the overnight ladder is that it needs no decisions. Two of
the four rules above require the platform to make decisions on the user's behalf, and question 2 of
the trader's §10 ("can your platform leave a conditional order overnight, unattended?") is
unanswered. If the answer is no, §7's already-thin economics are not merely thin, they are
unavailable.

Every rule takes the **delta cap** as a hard override (`run_rule(..., cap=)`), and the scorers report
how often it binds. On the reference book it binds constantly — see §8.

## 4. Three control bugs, each of which changed the answer

`docs/10` §6.1 records two control bugs that each manufactured an effect, and warns that this is the
characteristic failure mode of this kind of study. Three more were found here. Two of them
manufactured an effect; one hid one. All three are in the module's docstrings so they cannot be
reintroduced quietly.

**4.1 — The ratchet silently degenerated into a symmetric band.** The obvious implementation returns
the band `ref ± h` as the trigger when the rule is unarmed. On close-sampled data the arming
threshold and the fill threshold are then the same level, so the rule *fills on the arming bar* and
is byte-identical to `SymmetricBand`. Every give-back produced the same number, which is what gave it
away. Unarmed, the ratchet must have **no fill level at all** — only the delta cap.

**4.2 — Comparing a ratchet at `h` against a symmetric band at the same `h` manufactures a positive
result on a random walk.** The first comparison "showed" the ratchet earning **+27 USD a night at
`phi = 0`**, where the expected gain is provably zero (§1). The explanation is mundane: a trailing
rule hedges less often, so it is **a wider band in disguise**, and at retail costs a wider band saves
money for reasons that have nothing to do with trend. A symmetric band widened to the cap earned
**+28** on the same paths — the same number. The fix is `ratchet.match_symmetric`: solve for the
symmetric `h*` that carries the *same mean delta* and score against that. Under matching, the
random-walk gain collapses to **−2.9 ± 5.4**, i.e. zero, as it must.

**4.3 — A wrong variance-ratio formula made every night look trending.** `session_stats` first
computed `vr = n * d2 / qv`. The correct per-session estimator is `vr = d2 / qv` (equivalently
`kappa = qv/d2`, `docs/10` §5.1). The bug inflated every reading by a factor of 13 and would have
had the tool declaring a strong trend regime every single night.

**A fourth trap, not a bug:** the aggregate estimator is **biased under the null in small samples**.
Pooling 13-bar sessions, `sum(d2)/sum(qv)` reads **0.95-1.03** under a generator whose true `VR` is
exactly 1.0, depending on session length and pooling. Comparisons must therefore be made against a
**simulated null, never against the number 1.0** — the same point `docs/10` §5.3 makes when it says
`kappa` between 0.9 and 1.1 should be read as "Brownian".

---

## 5. Is intraday persistence *detectable*? Yes — but never in one night

`ratchet.ar1_paths`, 40,000 replications. The statistic is the session variance ratio `d2/qv`.

**One session of 14 hourly bars, under the random-walk null:**

| bars in the session | mean | median | sd | 5% | 95% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 13 (hourly, one night) | 0.98 | 0.49 | **1.25** | 0.004 | 3.65 |
| 27 (30-minute bars) | 1.00 | 0.48 | 1.34 | 0.004 | 3.73 |
| 167 (5-minute bars) | 1.00 | 0.46 | 1.40 | 0.004 | 3.89 |

**Sampling finer does not help.** The estimator's noise is driven by the *number of independent
window-length moves*, which is one, no matter how finely you slice it. This is the single most
important number in this document: **a single night's variance ratio has a standard deviation of
1.25 around a mean of 1.0 and a median of 0.49.** A night that "looks like a trend" is almost always
a coin.

**Classification accuracy from one night** (calling the sign of `phi` correctly, 0.5 = a coin):

| true \|φ\| | from 1 session | from 20 pooled sessions |
|---|---|---|
| 0.05 | 0.524 | 0.621 |
| 0.10 | 0.547 | 0.734 |
| 0.20 | 0.595 | 0.893 |
| 0.30 | 0.640 | 0.972 |

**Pooling works.** The aggregate over K sessions has sd 0.60 at K=5, **0.303 at K=20**, 0.087 at
K=250. So persistence *is* detectable — as a **property of the pair measured over months**, not as a
property of tonight. That distinction is the whole result: a stable property does not need a
forecast, it needs a measurement, and if you have measured it you set the band once and leave it.

---

## 6. Is it *forecastable*? No — and the null control passes

Walk-forward, 19,960 scored nights per row, trailing K=20 sessions, no look-ahead. The true `phi`
follows a two-state Markov chain `{+a, -a}` with mean duration D nights. Forecast: the trailing
20-session aggregate VR. Decision: use the ratchet when `VR_hat > 1`, else the symmetric band.
Money is USD per night on the reference book at the trader's 0.6-pip all-in cost.

| true process | R² vs Brownian null | R² vs trailing mean | corr(v̂, realised) | switch rule vs symmetric |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **φ = 0 (NULL CONTROL)** | −0.057 | −0.057 | −0.002 | **+0.45 ± 2.84** |
| φ = ±0.2, iid each night | −0.057 | −0.060 | −0.005 | −1.15 ± 3.11 |
| φ = ±0.2, regime lasts ~5 nights | −0.061 | −0.063 | +0.008 | +3.55 ± 3.12 |
| φ = ±0.2, regime lasts ~20 nights | −0.051 | −0.054 | +0.075 | +3.53 ± 3.17 |
| φ = +0.2 constant forever | −0.017 | −0.071 | −0.007 | +27.13 ± 4.15 |
| φ = +0.1 constant forever | −0.045 | −0.061 | +0.002 | +14.19 ± 3.61 |
| φ = +0.05 constant (realistic ceiling) | −0.056 | −0.059 | +0.002 | +4.37 ± 3.23 |

Read it in this order:

- **The null control passes.** At `phi = 0` the switching rule earns +0.45 ± 2.84 — nothing. If this
  row had been positive, everything else in the document would have been a bug.
- **`R²` against the Brownian null is negative in all seven cells** — including the cells where the
  true persistence is large and *constant*. This is `docs/10` §5.4's daily-bar result reproduced at
  hourly frequency, and for the same reason: the target for one night is 92% noise (§5), so
  multiplying a good baseline by an estimate of the signal makes it worse. Hourly data fixes the
  *measurement* problem (§10) and does **not** fix the *forecasting* problem.
- **The only cells where switching earns anything are the ones where there is nothing to forecast.**
  When `phi` is constant, the trailing estimate is just a measurement of a fixed property; the
  switching machinery adds nothing over always-on (+27 vs +34), and you would set the band once.
- **In the genuinely regime-switching cells (D = 5 and D = 20), the switch earns +3.5 ± 3.1** —
  indistinguishable from zero, on a true effect of ±0.2 that is far larger than anything liquid FX
  displays at hourly frequency.

---

## 7. Conditional performance and regime misidentification — the centrepiece

The reference book: EURUSD 1M straddle, `gamma_1pct = EUR 3.91mm`, `G = 335.6mm`, spot 1.1650,
delta per pip EUR 33.6k, theta USD 3,978/day (**USD 2,321 over the 14-hour window**). Window sigma
0.2726% = 31.8 pips (0.382 of a day's variance, `docs/10` §3). Continuous-hedging gamma P&L over the
window: **USD 1,692** — which the simulation reproduces at 1,693, and which is *less than the
theta*, exactly the negative-carry point that leads the overnight screen.

Delta cap **EUR 1.0mm = 30 pips**; clip floor EUR 0.5mm = 15 pips; base band 20 pips. For context,
`bandopt.optimal_band` at `risk_aversion=1e-6` returns 59 pips (interbank), 103 pips (0.6-pip
all-in) and 175 pips (repo retail table) — **all far outside the cap, so the cap binds and the
analytic band never decides anything.** That is the trader's §4.2/§4.3 point, confirmed.

### 7.1 The table that decides it

`ratchet.matched_comparison`, 12,000 nights per cell, cost 1.03bp (0.6 pips all-in), cap EUR 1.0mm.
Each cell scores `Ratchet(h=20p, give_back=0.5)` against **its own risk-matched symmetric band** —
the band that carries the same mean delta, which comes out at 28-29 pips, i.e. at the cap.

| true φ | VR(13) | matched band | **ratchet vs matched band, USD/night** | t | p95 \|delta\| | matched p95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **−0.30** | 0.566 | 27.7p | **−68.6** ± 5.3 | −13.0 | 0.98mm | 0.91mm |
| **−0.20** | 0.688 | 28.1p | **−40.9** ± 5.2 | −7.9 | 0.99 | 0.93 |
| **−0.10** | 0.831 | 28.4p | **−24.6** ± 5.5 | −4.5 | 0.99 | 0.94 |
| −0.05 | 0.912 | 28.4p | −10.0 ± 5.7 | −1.8 | 0.99 | 0.94 |
| **0.00** | 1.000 | 28.6p | **−2.9** ± 5.4 | −0.5 | 0.99 | 0.95 |
| +0.05 | 1.097 | 28.7p | +4.7 ± 5.4 | +0.9 | 0.99 | 0.95 |
| **+0.10** | 1.203 | 28.8p | **+17.7** ± 5.5 | +3.2 | 0.99 | 0.95 |
| +0.15 | 1.321 | 28.8p | +32.4 ± 5.6 | +5.8 | 0.99 | 0.95 |
| **+0.20** | 1.452 | 28.9p | **+31.5** ± 5.4 | +5.8 | 0.99 | 0.96 |
| **+0.30** | 1.763 | 29.1p | **+52.3** ± 5.3 | +10.0 | 0.99 | 0.96 |

The payoff is linear in the persistence to `R² = 0.99`:

```
ratchet edge  =  199 * phi  -  3.8      USD per night      (break-even phi = +0.019)
```

**This is the answer to the question.** The rule is not a hedging improvement; it is **a bet on
`phi`, priced at USD 199 per unit of `phi` per night**, and it is very nearly antisymmetric: the
money you make when the regime is a trend is the money you lose when it is chop. Combine it with §6
— you cannot tell which regime tonight is — and the expectation of trading it is the expectation of
`phi` itself, which for liquid FX at hourly frequency is approximately zero.

### 7.2 What it costs when the regime is called wrong

Read the table as a confusion matrix. Call trend, get chop:

- at `phi = −0.10` (a mild chop, the common case in liquid FX): **−25 USD a night**;
- at `phi = −0.30`: **−69 USD a night**, against a whole-night gamma P&L of USD 1,195 — **5.7% of
  the night's gamma P&L, handed back for calling the regime wrong**;
- and the loss is taken while carrying more delta: p95 `|delta|` 0.98mm against the matched band's
  0.91mm, with the cap binding on 32-46% of nights against 9-18% for the 20-pip symmetric band.

For scale, the trader put the **entire** band decision at ~USD 60 a night and the ladder's whole
cost range across every plausible band at USD 81. The ratchet's regime bet is the same size as the
decision the trader already called not worth optimising — and unlike the band, it has a sign that
depends on something unknowable.

### 7.3 The other two rules do nothing

Same experiment, 6,000 nights, matched:

- `TimeAndState(widen 1.3, tighten 0.8)`: **+2.8, +4.1, +0.6, +2.4, −0.1** USD/night across
  φ = +0.3 → −0.3. Zero everywhere, |t| < 1.1. Two consecutive same-sign legs is too weak a state signal to act on:
  at a 20-pip band there are only ~1.5 legs in a night, so the state variable is usually undefined.
- `AsymmetricBand(+25% up / −25% down)`: **+20.6 ± 11.9** in the strongest trend and noise
  elsewhere; nothing reaches |t| = 2. A *static* tilt applied all night in one direction is a
  directional position, and this confirms the band agent's finding from the other side: their
  first-order condition returns a ×6.97 multiplier at φ=+0.3, which is the model being taken outside
  its range. A static persistence multiplier should not ship, and does not.

---

## 8. The give-back parameter, and the delta you end up holding

### 8.1 Give-back sweep

`ratchet.giveback_sensitivity`, 12,000 nights, versus a symmetric band at the **same** `h` = 20 pips
(so this table contains the band-widening effect of §4.2 on purpose — it is how the parameter
behaves, not evidence about trend):

| give-back | φ=+0.30 | φ=0 | φ=−0.30 | hedges/night | end \|delta\| |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.00 | +320 | +18.7 | −192 | 1.43 | 0.32mm |
| 0.25 | +305 | +22.0 | −173 | 1.35 | 0.34 |
| **0.50** | **+272** | **+25.5** | **−137** | 1.27 | 0.36 |
| 1.00 | +234 | +28.3 | −98 | 1.14 | 0.36 |
| 1.50 | +221 | +29.1 | −94 | 1.05 | 0.36 |
| 2.00 | +227 | +29.6 | −97 | 1.00 | 0.36 |

The give-back is an **insurance premium on the regime call**: a small give-back keeps the trend edge
(+320) and pays for it in chop (−192); a large one gives most of both away and the rule converges to
a static wide band (the φ=0 column converging on +29, which is the pure band-widening number of
§4.2). There is no interior optimum that is not a view on `phi`. The `phi=0` column being *flat and
positive* across the whole sweep is the tell: whatever you set the give-back to, the part of the
answer that does not depend on the regime is band width, and you can get that from the band.

### 8.2 Delta carried — the thing the cap exists to limit

Distribution of `|delta|` (EUR mm), random-walk paths, cap EUR 1.0mm:

| quantile | symmetric 20p (any time / at open) | symmetric 28.6p | ratchet g=0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50% | 0.19 / 0.21 | 0.27 / 0.32 | 0.25 / 0.30 |
| 90% | 0.52 / 0.53 | 0.71 / 0.74 | 0.73 / 0.77 |
| 95% | 0.58 / 0.60 | 0.81 / 0.85 | **0.84 / 0.87** |
| 99% | 0.65 / 0.66 | 0.92 / 0.93 | **0.97 / 0.97** |

At a **matched mean** delta the ratchet still carries more in the tail — it concentrates its delta
into exactly the moves that are running. That is the mechanism working as designed, and it is also
the definition of the risk the cap exists to bound. On the reference book the 99th percentile
morning delta goes from EUR 0.66mm (20-pip band) to EUR 0.97mm: on a further 30-pip gap that is
USD 900 more of overnight P&L the user did not choose.

**And the cap is what actually decides the band.** With a EUR 1.0mm cap the usable range for any
dynamic rule is the gap between the 15-pip clip floor and the 30-pip cap — a factor of two. If the
band is set at the cap, as the band agent recommends, a trend-conditional widening has **nowhere to
go**: `Ratchet(h=cap)` is identical to `SymmetricBand(cap)`. The freedom this whole workstream is
arguing over is one factor of two inside a constraint the user sets for other reasons entirely.

---

## 9. Could the user ever verify this on their own book? No

Per-night standard deviation of the paired difference (ratchet minus matched band): **USD 593**.
Nights needed to establish the P&L edge at t = 2, and the nights needed merely to *detect* the
persistence (VR ≠ 1 at 2 se, from §5's K=20 sd of 0.303):

| φ | edge, USD/night | nights to establish the edge | years | nights to detect the persistence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| +0.05 | 6.1 | 37,444 | **149** | 785 (3.1 yr) |
| +0.10 | 16.1 | 5,450 | **21.6** | 178 (0.7 yr) |
| +0.15 | 26.0 | 2,080 | 8.3 | 71 |
| +0.20 | 36.0 | 1,089 | 4.3 | 36 |
| +0.30 | 55.8 | 452 | 1.8 | 13 |

At any persistence a liquid FX pair plausibly displays at hourly frequency, **the amount of data
needed to prove the rule pays is a career, and the amount needed even to measure the persistence is
years — over which no one would claim it is stable.** The one honest use of this arithmetic is the
reverse: it says how big `phi` would have to be before the question is worth revisiting, and the
answer is `phi >= +0.15`, i.e. `VR(13) >= 1.32`. Nothing in liquid G10 FX at hourly frequency is
remotely near that.

### 9.1 Cross-check through the shipped backtest engine

`ratchet.backtest_with_rule` mirrors `backtest.engine.run_backtest` with a pluggable trigger.
`ratchet.verify_against_engine` proves the mirror is faithful: with the engine's own band rule it
reproduces `run_backtest` **bit for bit** (`max_abs_equity_diff = 0.0`, `max_abs_cost_diff = 0.0`,
identical hedge counts) on both `band` and `time` modes, so the costs below are charged by the
shipped accounting and the option marks are the shipped pricer's.

24 paired runs, 90 days of hourly bars, 30-day straddle rolled, cost 1.03bp, cap EUR 1.0mm:

| true φ | symmetric net | ratchet net | difference | se | t | per day |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.0 | −26,844 | −37,225 | **−10,380** | 6,931 | −1.5 | −115 |
| +0.2 | +24,391 | +29,668 | **+5,277** | 4,544 | +1.2 | +59 |

The signs agree with §7 and **neither is significant**. That is not a failure of the experiment, it
is the point restated in the units the user would experience: on a real option book, over a quarter,
the effect is invisible underneath the book's own P&L. Anyone who runs this rule for three months
and concludes it works has measured noise.

---

## 10. What the intraday module actually delivers

`fxgamma/data/intraday_yahoo.py` — Yahoo's chart endpoint at `interval=1h` (and finer), the same
free, no-key API as `spot_yahoo`, following the same `fetch_*` / `parse_*` split. **Status:
UNVERIFIED** — every market-data host is blocked by this sandbox's egress proxy, so the fetch path
has never run; the parser is fixture-tested against `sample_payload()`, a recorded-shape envelope
whose prices are generated and which deliberately contains a null bar, a duplicate timestamp and a
weekend gap. `VERIFIED = False` until `check_live()` is run from a machine with egress.

Design points that are not decoration:

- **Lookback caps are enforced, not hoped for.** Yahoo serves ~730 days of hourly, ~60 days of
  5-minute, ~7 days of 1-minute, and beyond the cap it silently returns a *shorter* series rather
  than an error. `intraday_history` clamps and warns; `parse_intraday` **raises** if
  `meta.dataGranularity` disagrees with the request, because Yahoo's response to an over-long window
  is to downgrade the granularity, and daily bars quietly mixed into an hourly frame is the worst
  failure mode available here.
- **Gaps are exposed, never interpolated.** `bar_gaps` found 104 gaps in 730 days of the synthetic
  feed, all 104 correctly classified as weekends. A non-weekend gap is a holiday or a data hole, and
  the repo still has **no holiday calendar** (`docs/10` §4.2, CR-16, still open).
- **Sessions are cut in the user's local timezone**, not UTC: they leave at 17:00 London, and half
  the year that is not 16:00 UTC.

What it unlocks, measured (`docs/10` §5.2's convergence question, run on 730 days of bars):

| grid | hourly count | fraction of the analytic baseline | daily count | fraction | hourly/daily |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 25 pips | 1,579 | **0.70** | 719 | 0.32 | **2.20x** |
| 50 pips | 488 | **0.87** | 276 | 0.49 | 1.77x |

Hourly bars see **1.8-2.2x more of the true crossing count** than daily bars do, which is exactly
the gap `docs/10` said had to be closed before roughness could be measured honestly — and it is
closed. `estimate_hour_profile` on the same frame produces a session variance fraction of **0.4212**
for London 17:00→07:00 against the clock's 0.583, and `estimate_persistence` on 520 pooled sessions
returns `VR(13) = 1.024 ± 0.049 -> indistinguishable from a random walk`, which is the right answer
for a generator built with `phi = 0`.

**Both of those are machinery checks, not market facts** (`docs/10` §0). The 0.4212 recovers the
profile that was fed in; the VR recovers the persistence that was fed in. They prove the pipeline
computes what it claims, which is what an air-gapped build can prove, and nothing more.

---

## 11. What to run on real data, and what would change the verdict

Once the hourly feed is reachable (30 minutes of work, no keys):

```python
from fxgamma.data import intraday_yahoo as iy
from fxgamma.portfolio import ratchet as rt

df, prov = iy.get_intraday("EURUSD", source="yahoo", interval="1h", days=730)
sess    = iy.overnight_sessions(df)                    # ~500 London-close -> open windows
stats   = iy.session_stats(sess, "EURUSD")
print(stats["d2"].sum() / stats["qv"].sum())           # the pooled variance ratio
rt.estimate_persistence(returns=..., block=13)         # with its own standard error
```

**The evidence bar for turning any of this on.** All five, and the conjunction is deliberate because
any one of them will be met by chance somewhere in a grid of pairs and horizons:

1. the pooled overnight `VR(13)` is **above 1.15** — not merely above 1 — on the user's own hourly
   history, with the Lo-MacKinlay z above 2;
2. it holds with the **same sign on at least three pairs**, because a single pair at z=2 is one test
   out of the many that will be run;
3. it holds in **both halves** of the sample, split by date;
4. the null comparator is a **simulated null on the same session lengths**, never the number 1.0
   (§4.4);
5. the implied edge, `199 * phi` USD a night on this book, is larger than the user's own all-in cost
   uncertainty — which at 15-40x the interbank table it currently is not.

**What would change the verdict wholesale:** a demonstration that overnight `VR` is *predictable*
night to night — a trailing estimator with positive `R²` against the Brownian null on the user's own
sessions, which is precisely the test in §6 that fails in all seven cells here. Run
`roughness_walk_forward` from `signals.rangeforecast` on hourly bars; it needs no new code.

**What would change nothing:** a good backtest of the ratchet over a few months. §9.1 shows the
effect is invisible at that sample size, so such a backtest can only measure noise, and a positive
one should be assumed to be §4.2 in a new costume.

## 12. Verdict table

| component | verdict | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| The trend/chop asymmetry in the gamma kernel | **REAL** — reproduced, and exactly equal to the return autocovariance | §1, §2 |
| `SymmetricBand` at the delta cap | **USE. This is the recommendation.** | §7, §8.2 |
| `AsymmetricBand` from **book skew** | **USE** — repricing, not a view; the rule prints the reason | trader `docs/11` §9.3 |
| `AsymmetricBand` from a **persistence tilt** | **DO NOT USE** — nothing reaches \|t\|=2 in any regime; gated on significance in code and off by default | §7.3 |
| `Ratchet` | **AVAILABLE, OFF.** A bet on `phi` at 199 USD/night per unit `phi`; −25/night at φ=−0.10 | §7.1, §7.2 |
| `TimeAndState` | **AVAILABLE, OFF** — measures zero in every regime | §7.3 |
| A static persistence band multiplier | **DO NOT SHIP** — agrees with the band agent's ×6.97 blow-up | §7.3 |
| Forecasting persistence for tonight | **DO NOT USE** — loses to the Brownian null in 7/7 cells, hourly data included | §6 |
| Measuring persistence from **pooled** hourly sessions | **USE** — it is detectable at K≥20 nights and it is an input the user can override | §5 |
| `intraday_yahoo` parser + session/gap/profile tooling | **USE**, badged UNVERIFIED | §10 |
| `intraday_yahoo` live fetch | **UNVERIFIED** — hosts blocked; run `check_live()` from outside | §10 |

**One sentence for the screen:** *"Persistence is detectable over months and unforecastable for
tonight; the symmetric band at your delta cap is the right answer, and the trailing rule is a
momentum bet worth about ±USD 30 a night on a coin flip."*

## 13. Reproducing every number here

`PYTHONPATH=/home/user/fx`, all offline, no network.

| § | call |
|---|---|
| 2 | `ratchet.pm_table(n_paths=4000, n_steps=240, seed=20260909)` (and `include_open_leg=True`) |
| 1 | `ratchet.capture_decomposition(path, rule)` — `residual` must be 0 |
| 5 | `ratchet.ar1_paths` + the session VR; 40,000 replications |
| 6 | walk-forward over `ratchet.ar1_price_paths` with a Markov `phi`, trailing K=20 |
| 7 | `ratchet.matched_comparison(paths, rules, gamma=335_622_318, cost_bp=1.03, cap_spot=30e-4, stat="mean_abs_delta", hi=30e-4)` |
| 8 | `ratchet.giveback_sensitivity`, `ratchet.delta_profile` |
| 9.1 | `ratchet.verify_against_engine(path, cfg)` then `ratchet.backtest_with_rule(...)` |
| 10 | `intraday_yahoo.synthetic_intraday` → `overnight_sessions` → `session_stats`; `rangeforecast.grid_crossings` on hourly vs resampled daily |

The two checks to run first if anything ever stops reproducing are `capture_decomposition`
(residual must be exactly 0) and `verify_against_engine` (all differences must be exactly 0). If
those pass and the market results move, the data changed. If they fail, the code did.
